Canadian targeted Taylor-rule estimates show policy responds more strongly to demand-driven than supply-driven inflation. Baseline coefficient remains model-scaled until the paper coefficient can be mapped one-for-one.
Same targeted Taylor-rule evidence constrains the response-function design but does not justify silently transplanting a differently normalized coefficient.
Canadian regime-switching evidence finds core inflation persistence very low under inflation targeting; used as empirical support for bounded persistence rather than a direct numerical transplant.

Bank research estimates a Canadian 12-quarter Phillips multiplier near 0.27. The simulator coefficient is a one-quarter equation slope, so the evidence constrains the envelope but is not numerically identical.

Canadian firm-level estimates imply economically meaningful exchange-rate pass-through. Simulator coefficient uses CAD/USD level deviation, so direct replacement requires a consistent elasticity-to-level conversion.
Canadian retaliatory-tariff study estimates roughly one-quarter pass-through of a 25% tariff to affected retail prices. Aggregate CPI mapping remains distinct from product-level pass-through.
